A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RouteT2I, with matching core methods and experiments despite the changed title. The text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 additionally supplies Appendices A–H, which were included in the assessment.

before.justification: V1 reports original COCO routing experiments, comparisons with other routers, results across ten generator pairs, and component ablations in Section 6.

after.justification: V2 retains original routing experiments and adds LAION results, preference-model scoring, prompt-complexity analysis, additional generator-pair comparisons, and measured deployment costs.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 retain the contrastive quality scores, PRS normalization and aggregation, dual-gate token-selection MoE, projection and score matrices, multiple prediction heads, and threshold-based routing. Added explanations and generator configurations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates COCO2014 captions only. V2 adds training and evaluation on LAION2B-en-aesthetic prompts (Appendix F), extending coverage from concise object descriptions to more colloquial and stylistic requests. The text-to-image routing task remains the same.

E2.justification: The baseline families remain RouteLLM-BERT, RouteLLM-MF, Hybrid LLM, ZOOTER, and random routing. However, v1 compares the learned baselines only for SD3/SD2.1, while its other generator-pair results report RouteT2I alone. V2 Appendix Tables 6–14 add all four learned baselines to those nine already-tested pairs, substantially expanding comparator participation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce a 20,000-training/10,000-validation LAION split, HPSv2 and MPS scoring at 50% routing, ImageReward analysis by noun count, and Jetson deployment measurements. Generator configurations expand from ten to eighteen pairs, including PixArt-α and Infinity. The stated optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and approximately ten training epochs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an empirical test of prompt complexity versus generator quality gaps (Figures 2–3), validation against preference-scoring models (Appendix D), and visual routing case studies (Appendix G). Appendix H also analyzes behavior across encoder and generator architectures. The original three component ablations and their Table 6 values are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 3 introduces shaded bands around the noun-count curves, but neither its caption nor the text identifies what the bands represent or how they were estimated. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts. The bands therefore cannot reliably be classified as a documented change in statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The headline SD3/SD2.1 results and ablation values remain, but Table 5 revises existing entries: SD3/SDXL at 40% routing changes from 27.10% to 29.78%. V2 adds LAION results, preference scores, additional pair comparisons, and runtime/memory measurements; v1's pairwise win-rate matrix is removed. These are revised and expanded reported results, without evidence establishing an underlying method improvement.

T1.justification: New Appendix B formalizes text and image space cardinalities, defines their logarithmic size ratio, and derives numerical comparisons for CLIP and T5 inputs. V1 only gives the qualitative space-size argument. This is a limited mathematical addition; the core routing equations are retained, and no routing optimality proof is added.

C1.justification: V1's contribution list claims a proposed contrastive multi-metric quality measure. V2 emphasizes the routing architecture built around multi-metric measures, while Section 4 attributes contrastive scoring to prior work. This narrows the novelty positioning of one component while retaining the central text-to-image routing and dual-gate MoE contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning preference alignment, edge-device suitability, customizable metrics, and semantic robustness across encoders. It removes v1's discussion of diminishing routing benefits at high cloud-routing rates. Its new description of 83.97% as a fraction of the full cloud gain is also imprecise: under the unchanged ΔP formula, v1 Table 2 assigns the cloud itself 80%, rather than 100%.

D1.justification: V2 discloses all ten positive/negative quality-prompt pairs, previously illustrated with only two examples. It adds generator and encoder specifications, explains baseline adaptation, and reports router size, training time, memory use, deployment hardware, and LAION sample counts. These materially expand reproducibility information. V1's statement that generators use official default hyperparameters is dropped.

R1.justification: V2 substantially strengthens grounding of the central components: contrastive scoring is attributed to Liang et al. and Wang et al.; metric selection is connected to HEIM, T2I-Scorer, and VisionPrefer; and MoE positioning adds token-mixture and expert-choice work. Related-work discussion further distinguishes T2I from LLM routing, alongside references supporting the new evaluations.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most method exposition remain. V2 revises the title and authorship information, adds acknowledgments, edits related-work and results prose, clarifies metric terminology, and organizes additional material into Appendices A–H. These are targeted editorial and structural refinements rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, adds prompt examples and complexity plots, removes v1's pairwise win-rate heatmap, and narrows the displayed routing-rate range in the performance curves. It restructures and expands the generator-pair table and adds extensive appendix tables and a routing-example image grid. The architecture diagram is retained with renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation through LAION evaluation, preference-scoring models outside the routing objective, broader baseline comparisons, and measured Jetson deployment costs. The complete quality-prompt specification also improves reproducibility. Unexplained score revisions, undefined uncertainty bands, and imprecise normalized-gain interpretations remain weaknesses, but the new evidence materially strengthens assessment of generalization, quality alignment, and practical feasibility.
